title: Go Nagai. Dante UFO Robot: "Run, lad, down there… to Hell!"
excerpt: It is not just about robots. The great Japanese master, creator of Goldrake and Devilman, who is coming to Lucca Comics & Games, tells us his take on the D…
content:
There is a specific date when the collective imagination of Italians underwent a transformation: 4 April 1978, when public television broadcast the first episode of *Atlas Ufo Robot*, better known to us as *Goldrake*, bringing into the homes of millions of children something they had never seen before: a giant anthropomorphic robot equipped with weapons that have also remained etched in the memory of several generations, such as the ‘Space Halberd’ and the ‘Piercing Mallet’, whose translations from Japanese were almost always made up. The theme tune also contributed to its success; its music and arrangements were created by maestro Vince Tempera, long-time leader of Francesco Guccini’s band ‘I Musici’, with the contribution of Ares Tavolazzi, formerly the (extraordinary) bassist of Area, a militant band and one of the most original on the ‘prog’ scene, not only in Italy.

It was a veritable sensation, the beginning of an era dominated by giant robots piloted by humans, from Mazinger to Jeeg, which redefined the concept of science fiction for entire generations. But to reduce Go Nagai’s legacy to this alone would be to ignore the complexity of one of the 20th century’s most radical visionaries, capable of breaking down taboos in both Japan and Italy by blending eroticism, violence and a crystal-clear philosophical and political reflection.

Having grown up in the wake of the ‘god of manga’ Osamu Tezuka – for whom he has always harboured absolute reverence – Nagai left his mark on post-war Japan by laying bare the hypocrisies of bourgeois respectability, first through the anarchic and irreverent humour of *Harenchi Gakuen* (*School Without Shame*), then by redefining the myth of metamorphosis with the polymorphous heroines of *Cutie Honey*.

But it was precisely when the master’s gaze ventured into the deepest darkness that his artistic journey reached its highest peaks, touching upon the perennial unease of the human condition: in 1971, Mao Dante was born, in which Go Nagai’s childhood fascination with Gustave Doré’s engravings merged with the destruction of the traditional canon. The demon trapped in ice and subsequently freed ceases, in fact, to be the pure embodiment of Evil, becoming instead the guardian of a truth suppressed by the victors, overturning the dichotomy between Light and Darkness, between God and the rebellious Angel, in an interpretation very close to that of Gnosticism. From that primordial matrix sprang, the following year, his absolute masterpiece, Devilman. Here the struggle between humans and devils ceases to be a superheroic fable and transforms into an apocalyptic tragedy, where the true horror lies not in the mutated flesh of the demons but in the ferocity, paranoia and racism that devour the souls of men when they are overcome by fear.

This prolonged struggle with the abyss could only lead him back to the original source of his obsession: with his monumental comic-book adaptation (over 600 pages, expanding to 776 in the special edition for Lucca Comics, including critical notes and previously unpublished artwork) of the Divine Comedy, completed in the 1990s, Nagai ideally brings things full circle. His work is not merely an academic homage to the Supreme Italian Poet, but a visionary and immensely powerful descent into the underworld that restores Dante Alighieri’s journey to its most human, carnal and desperate dimension. To mark his return to Lucca Comics and to the adopted homeland of the father of the Italian language, Go Nagai reveals here the common thread that links the hearts of human beings, the steel of robots, the tears of demons and the eternal quest for redemption.

Before turning to Dante Alighieri, what was your relationship with Western literature and culture?

‘Dante’s Divine Comedy, Carlo Collodi’s Pinocchio, Vittorio De Sica’s Bicycle Thieves, Federico Fellini’s La Strada, Jean-Jacques Annaud’s The Name of the Rose, Visconti’s The Leopard, Ladislao Vajda’s Marcellino, Bread and Wine, and so on: the list of European works I came into contact with as a boy would be endless. I first encountered Dante around Year 4 or 5 of primary school, in a children’s book illustrated by Gustave Doré: I was literally overwhelmed and captivated by the charm of that spiritual vision and by the pictorial imagination of that monstrous and fantastical world.”

How long did it take you to create your *Commedia*, and how did you approach the Catholic Church’s moral division between Good and Evil?

“I think it took me six months for the first volume and then, with a few breaks in between, about two years to illustrate the entire three-volume work. Broadly speaking, I tried to do justice to the original text and, as regards the overall visual presentation, I started with the idea of drawing inspiration from Doré’s engravings. To heighten the visual impact, I chose to depict Cerberus and the ferryman Charon as gigantic creatures, so as to convey a sense of imminent danger for Dante. As for the moral aspect, given that this is a world built upon a very specific religious vision, I felt it was important to respect it and leave it intact.’

In your stories, there is often a young person who discovers they are not entirely human and bears that burden. Does Dante, lost in Hell in search of himself, resemble your heroes? And how did the idea for ‘Mao Dante’ come about, long before the adaptation?

‘Dante is deeply akin to my characters, in his very essence, because I believe that human beings live with a soul that is inherently imperfect. The idea for *Mao Dante* arose from a desire to draw a manga about giant monsters modelled on Godzilla; I realised, however, that it would merely be a copy. I then thought that, by drawing inspiration from the image of the demon imprisoned in the ice of the Cocytus in Dante’s *Inferno*, I could create something entirely original. I used the Lucifer from the*Divine Comedy* as the model for the creature: I named him Dante because I wanted to pay homage to Dante Alighieri’s masterpiece, linking the character to it. It was absolutely not my intention to compare the two figures (‘Ma-O’ literally means ‘King of the Underworld’, ed.). I simply started from the idea of what a threat that demon might pose to modern society, should he manage to escape from that icy prison.’

The demon in *Mao Dante* challenges the very concept of Good and Evil. In your view, are there objective criteria for judging the guilty? How does this concept evolve in the subsequent *Devilman*?

‘History is written by the victors: I harboured the thought that perhaps even those labelled as demons – that is, the vanquished – might have their own idea of justice. Just as happens in the modern age, everyone fights convinced they are in the right; the vanquished are branded as evil and end up buried in the darkness of history. Mao Dante tackled the theme of how monsters are born; for Devilman, however, the television anime series was the priority, and I was asked to create a demonic character who was also a hero. Whilst drawing him, I thought that focusing on the ‘society’ that creates demons would make the narrative far more interesting.”

In Devilman the greatest horror is the savagery that erupts among men when all certainty crumbles. Who are the real monsters: the demons or ourselves?

‘Monsters are the madness and cruelty that every human being hides deep within their heart: I believe this is precisely why wars never disappear from the world, and this is the “monster” par excellence. I think every single person must lock away and keep at bay the beast they carry within themselves. The focus on fear stems precisely from the fact that when people are overcome by it, they end up losing control, setting themselves on the path to ruin… Racism, collective panic, the need to create an enemy: I believe that human beings are the sum of all these things. And I also think that each of us bears a share of the blame: that is why I consider it essential that people, whatever circumstances they find themselves in, never take that step that leads to the abyss.”

The world of Devilman plunges into utter chaos, transforming the apocalypse into a dramatic tale of war. Is this a work that resonates with what is happening today?

‘I drew Devilman precisely with this in mind: I believe that today, in various countries, there are leaders intent on destroying the established order, and it was precisely with the aim of sounding the alarm that I created that work.’

In your works, divinity is often portrayed as a hostile, distant power to be openly defied. What is your personal relationship with religion?

“Driven by the question of whether it is truly right to believe blindly in God, or whether one should instead exercise one’s own critical judgement, I deliberately chose to portray God from an opposing perspective. The great spiritual questions attract me, and I wanted to depict them because I am captivated by them; I do not profess any specific religion, but I believe in God as a marvellous presence. And I have faith that human beings can progress towards the good. Precisely for this reason, as a warning, I have depicted the exact opposite: I wanted readers to be able to reflect and develop their own personal awareness.’

And what do you think of robots being used as weapons: have your visions come true?

‘At the heart of all my works lies the same question: what is a human being? And today I feel strongly that reality is catching up with fantasy. The pace of the world is accelerating at a dizzying rate, and even the emergence of giant robotic weapons seems on the verge of becoming a reality. As for artificial intelligence, I do not use it myself, but I think the key is not to employ it in ways that create a crisis for our identity.”

Returning to your *Commedia*, Dante appears frightened, fragile, deeply human, escorted by Virgil and sustained by Beatrice’s love. Why did you choose to strip him of all grandeur, and what role do inner guides play for you?

‘Future generations tend to deify the great figures of the past because of the immensity of their legacy; but in reality, I believe that each of them was a human being who lived their life struggling with all their might, just like us. I believe that everyone has someone who came before them as a point of reference: we are always looking for a role model to aspire to. For me, for example, it was the master Osamu Tezuka. As for Beatrice, rather than thinking of her in relation to myself, I drew her with what she represented for Dante in mind: the figure capable of healing his soul, the eternal companion of his heart.’

Through robots, aliens, mutant monsters and weeping demons, what does manga manage to express that realism cannot convey? Can comics be as popular and universal as the vernacular was for Dante? And should the artist remain in the thick of things or become a detached observer? “Manga has the extraordinary ability to use extreme figures such as demons or monsters as clear metaphors to explore the human soul: I believe my readers have become passionate about it precisely because they sensed that even those monstrous creatures were expressions of our own nature. Furthermore, by proceeding through images and metaphors, manga allows each reader to interpret what they see; just like Dante’s vernacular, it is an art form capable of raising profound questions and conveying ‘something’ of depth to a vast audience without losing its essence. As for the artist’s role, I see myself as a critical observer, but I do not expect others to do the same.” After a career spent narrating apocalypses, how do you envisage the future and where do you think you’ll end up in the afterlife? “I have absorbed every lesson from Dante: the paths that a person can take in life are truly innumerable and the journeys are often painful, but I hope that sooner or later everyone will choose to set out towards hope. Hard and complex times certainly lie ahead, but I am confident that, in the end, a better future will come for everyone. And as for me… I believe I shall go to Heaven. Why? Simply because that is where I wish to go.”

EVENTS AND MEETINGS

From 28 October to 1 November, Lucca Comics & Games returns, an event spread across the city’s historic centre, which in 2026 will celebrate sixty years of history with an edition entitled ‘Legacy’. Five days of talks, shows and major international guests, covering comics, games, fiction, cinema, animation, video games and music. Among the most eagerly awaited guests at this year’s event is the master Go Nagai: the exhibition ‘Sun, Heart, Steel’ at the Fondazione del Monte is dedicated to him. The author will also be the guest at two events: on 28 October at the Teatro del Giglio at 3.00 pm with ‘Maxi Showcase’, a live drawing session open to the public, accompanied by iconic animation theme tunes. On Friday 30th at 10.30 am, the master will be in conversation with three special guests: the illustrator Claudio Castellini, the director Gabriele Mainetti and the blogger and writer Alessandro Apreda, alias DocManhattan. His *Divina Commedia Omnibus Variant* will be available at the JPOP Shop during the Fair, an exclusive edition for Lucca (776 pages, €29.90).
